static.topic: Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Elections, Electoral Reforms, Constitutional Bodies (Election Commission of India)
static.whatIsIt: SIR is a special, more intensive revision of an electoral roll ordered by the Election Commission of India, distinct from the routine annual summary revision. It involves house-to-house enumeration by Block Level Officers, door-to-door verification of existing electors, issue of notices, and disposal of claims (Form 6), objections (Form 7) and corrections (Form 8) by Electoral Registration Officers before draft and final rolls are published.
static.background: Electoral rolls in India are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950 and the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960. Section 21 of the 1950 Act empowers the ECI to order a special revision of the roll in any constituency or part of it. Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of elections in the ECI. SIR is not a new instrument — it has been used in the past, and was most recently conducted on a statewide scale in Bihar in 2025 before being extended to other States, including Telangana.
static.geography: Hyderabad district is the smallest district by area in Telangana and lies on the Deccan plateau along the Musi river; it is the State capital and a major destination for internal migrants from Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Odisha and other States employed in IT, pharma, construction and the informal service sector.
static.socioEconomic: Hyderabad's electorate includes a large share of tenants, daily-wage and migrant workers who often lack stable documentary proof of residence, making them vulnerable to non-inclusion or deletion during intensive verification drives. This is the core equity concern raised against SIR.
static.whyInNews: A district official stated that the SIR in Hyderabad district found no illegal immigrant on the electoral rolls, amid the ECI's ongoing intensive revision exercise in Telangana.
static.wayForward: Ensure that deletions are made only after due notice and a reasoned order, with clear and accessible appeal routes to the District Election Officer and Chief Electoral Officer; strengthen inter-agency data sharing for death and shift records; and run proactive enrolment camps so that eligible but under-documented voters are added rather than merely dropped.
prelimsPointers: Electoral rolls are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950; Section 21 empowers the ECI to order a special revision.
Article 324 vests superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and conduct of elections in the ECI.
The qualifying date for enrolment is 1 January, with 1 April, 1 July and 1 October also available for persons turning 18 during the year.
Article 326 provides for adult suffrage — elections to the Lok Sabha and State Assemblies on the basis of universal adult voting.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether intensive roll-revision exercises reconcile the ECI's mandate of a clean electoral roll with the constitutional guarantee of universal adult suffrage, and suggest procedural safeguards.

static.topic: Citizenship, Illegal Migration and the 'D-Voter' Framework
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Citizenship, Fundamental Rights, Union and State Legislature
static.whatIsIt: Indian citizenship is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955, which provides for citizenship by birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory. A foreign national present without valid documents is dealt with under the Foreigners Act, 1946 and the Passport (Entry into India) Act, 1920. In Assam, the ECI's electoral machinery marks a person as a 'Doubtful Voter' (D-voter) on a reference from the State government or the ECI, and such a person cannot vote until a Foreigners' Tribunal decides the case.
static.background: The D-voter category emerged in Assam in the 1990s in the context of large-scale illegal migration. The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019, and the National Register of Citizens exercise in Assam further sharpened the debate on identifying non-citizens. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that no person can be deprived of citizenship or voting rights without due process and an opportunity of being heard.
static.geography: The issue is most acute in Assam and the North-East because of a porous land border with Bangladesh; it has now become a wider political question in urban centres such as Hyderabad that attract large internal migration.
static.socioEconomic: Verification drives that conflate internal migrants with foreign nationals can disproportionately burden poor, tenant and informal-sector households who lack documentary proof of residence, creating a de facto exclusion from the electoral roll.
static.whyInNews: The Hyderabad district administration's statement that no illegal immigrant was found on the district's electoral rolls during SIR places the citizenship-versus-enrolment question at the centre of the current roll-revision debate.
static.wayForward: Keep electoral-roll verification and citizenship determination as separate processes with distinct legal thresholds; ensure that any reference on citizenship goes through the statutory tribunal route with notice, evidence and appeal, rather than through administrative deletion from the roll.
prelimsPointers: Citizenship in India is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955; the Constitution deals with citizenship only at the commencement of the Constitution (Part II, Articles 5–11).
The 'D-voter' category operates in Assam; a person so marked cannot vote until a Foreigners' Tribunal decides the case.
The Foreigners Act, 1946 places the burden of proving that a person is not a foreigner on the person concerned in specified circumstances.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss the constitutional and legal safeguards that must accompany any exercise to identify non-citizens on electoral rolls, and evaluate the risk of wrongful exclusion of genuine voters.

prelims: Electoral rolls are prepared under the Representation of the People Act, 1950; Section 21 allows the ECI to order a special revision of the roll.
Article 324 gives the ECI superintendence, direction and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections.
Article 326 guarantees elections on the basis of adult suffrage, i.e., every citizen not less than 18 years of age is entitled to be registered as a voter.
The 'D-voter' (Doubtful Voter) category exists in Assam; such a person loses voting rights until a Foreigners' Tribunal decides the case.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls aims at electoral integrity, but it also raises the risk of disenfranchising genuine voters. Examine the constitutional and statutory framework governing the revision of electoral rolls and suggest safeguards to balance the two objectives.

stories.headline: Cyclone Murasu spares Odisha, but Arnab floods leave farmers reeling
stories.summary: Cyclone Murasu passed Odisha without causing major damage, but the state is still recovering from flooding triggered by Cyclone Arnab, which devastated standing crops in the southern districts. Farmers there report heavy financial losses and say the compensation received so far is inadequate to cover input costs and lost income. Several villages continue to face power outages in the aftermath of the flooding. The Odisha government has ordered crop loss surveys to identify affected cultivators, while a central team has toured the state to assess the damage. The episode highlights the layered burden on coastal and agrarian communities when back-to-back cyclonic systems hit within a single season.
stories.whyItMatters: Cyclone-and-flood induced crop loss is a recurring test of India's disaster preparedness, relief financing and agrarian support systems — a direct link between GS-I physical geography, GS-II federal fiscal arrangements and GS-III agriculture.

perspectives.take: Frames the event through climate-vulnerability and farmer-distress lens, foregrounding inadequate compensation and slow recovery in Odisha's southern districts rather than the spared cyclone itself; typical of India-focused environmental journalism.

articles.title: Cyclone Murasu spares Odisha, but Arnab’s floods leave farmers struggling to recover
articles.snippet: Cyclone Murasu spared Odisha, but Cyclone Arnab's floods devastated crops in southern districts, leaving farmers struggling with financial losses and inadequate compensation. Villages face power outages, while a central team assesses damage. The Odisha government has ordered crop loss surveys to aid affected farmers.

static.topic: Tropical Cyclones and Monsoon Variability in the Bay of Bengal
static.syllabusNode: Geography — Physical Geography of India (Monsoon, Cyclones, Drainage)
static.whatIsIt: The Indian monsoon is a seasonal reversal of winds driven by differential heating, the northward shift of the ITCZ and the Tibetan Plateau's role as a heat pump, delivering roughly 75% of annual rainfall between June and September. Tropical cyclones forming over the warm Bay of Bengal are a distinct, high-impact component of this system, bringing intense rainfall, storm surge and inland flooding to India's eastern coast.
static.background: Monsoon strength is modulated by El Niño (usually weakening), La Niña (usually strengthening) and the Indian Ocean Dipole. Cyclones in the North Indian Ocean are named under the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones, with the IMD acting as the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre. Odisha's coastline, backed by the Eastern Ghats and deltaic plains of the Mahanadi system, is historically among India's most cyclone-exposed regions, which drove the state's shift towards pre-emptive evacuation and early-warning-based preparedness.
static.geography: Bay of Bengal basin; Odisha coast and its southern districts; deltaic and low-lying agrarian plains prone to riverine and flash flooding after cyclonic rainfall; Eastern Ghats influencing rainfall distribution.
static.socioEconomic: Predominantly rain-fed and cyclone-exposed agriculture supports a large share of Odisha's rural population; repeated crop loss pushes small and marginal farmers into debt, distress migration and dependence on relief rather than insurance.
static.whyInNews: Cyclone Murasu spared Odisha, but flooding associated with Cyclone Arnab caused severe crop damage in the state's southern districts, prompting crop loss surveys and a central damage-assessment visit.
static.wayForward: Strengthen multi-hazard early warning and last-mile dissemination, embed cyclone-resilient crop calendars and drainage infrastructure in coastal districts, and link relief disbursal timelines to verified crop loss surveys.
prelimsPointers: Himalayan rivers are perennial (snow-fed) while peninsular rivers are largely seasonal and rain-fed.
The Bay of Bengal records a far higher frequency of tropical cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
Cyclone names for the North Indian Ocean are assigned by the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones, coordinated by the IMD.
static.mainsAngle: Monsoon variability, cyclonic activity and climate change — evaluate India's disaster preparedness for floods and cyclones with reference to coastal states like Odisha.

static.topic: Crop Loss Compensation and Agrarian Support Systems
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Agriculture & Food Security (MSP, Procurement, Farmer Income)
static.whatIsIt: India's agricultural support architecture combines a Minimum Support Price announced on CACP recommendations for 22 mandated crops, food security guaranteed through the National Food Security Act, 2013 and PDS operations run by the FCI, and direct income support through PM-KISAN. Compensation for disaster-linked crop loss sits alongside these as a relief measure rather than a price or income guarantee.
static.background: The Green Revolution of the 1960s made India food-sufficient but concentrated procurement in wheat and paddy. The Shanta Kumar Committee (2015) reviewed FCI operations; PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 per year as income support; the three farm laws of 2020 were repealed in 2021. Disaster-linked crop loss relief is typically disbursed as input subsidy under state and national disaster relief norms, and its adequacy is a persistent farmer grievance.
static.socioEconomic: Small and marginal holdings dominate Indian agriculture; a single uninsured crop failure can wipe out a season's working capital, making timely and adequate compensation central to rural income stability.
static.whyInNews: Farmers in Odisha's flood-affected southern districts report financial losses and inadequate compensation after Cyclone Arnab, with the state ordering crop loss surveys to identify beneficiaries.
static.wayForward: Move from ad hoc relief to parametric or weather-index insurance, digitise and speed up crop loss assessment using remote sensing, and integrate compensation databases with PM-KISAN and land records for faster targeting.
prelimsPointers: MSP is a price assurance, not a legal right; procurement remains concentrated in wheat and paddy.
NFSA covers up to 75% of the rural and 50% of the urban population.
PM-KISAN provides ₹6,000 per year in direct income support to eligible farmer families.
static.mainsAngle: Reforming MSP and procurement while raising farmer incomes — examine whether disaster-linked crop loss compensation can be made predictable and adequate.

static.topic: Centre-State Coordination in Disaster Response
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution (Centre-State Relations)
static.whatIsIt: India is a quasi-federal union in which powers are divided between the Union and the States through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule, with residuary powers vested in the Union under Article 248. Disaster response operates within this division, requiring the Union and States to coordinate on assessment, funding and relief delivery.
static.background: The Sarkaria Commission (1983) and the Punchhi Commission (2007) examined Centre-State balance, including fiscal devolution and institutional coordination. The Governor (Article 153) acts as the Centre's constitutional representative and has been a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201). Disaster response adds a practical, non-partisan arena where cooperative federalism is tested through joint damage assessment and fund release.
static.socioEconomic: Delays in central assessment and fund release translate directly into delayed relief for affected households, deepening distress in already vulnerable coastal and agrarian districts.
static.whyInNews: A central team visited Odisha to assess flood damage from Cyclone Arnab while the state government ordered crop loss surveys — a live example of Centre-State coordination in disaster relief.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise time-bound joint damage assessment protocols, strengthen State Disaster Response Fund replenishment cycles, and use digital damage reporting to reduce disputes over relief quantum.
prelimsPointers: On a repugnancy between Union and State laws on a Concurrent List subject, the Union law prevails unless the State law has been reserved for and received the President's assent (Article 254).
The Inter-State Council (Article 263) is a recommendatory body for inter-state coordination and dispute resolution.
static.mainsAngle: Recent frictions over the Governor's assent and fiscal devolution — assess how cooperative federalism performs in practice, using disaster relief coordination as a case study.

prelims: Cyclone Murasu spared Odisha, but flooding linked to Cyclone Arnab damaged crops in the state's southern districts.
The Odisha government ordered crop loss surveys, and a central team assessed the flood damage.
Cyclone names in the North Indian Ocean are assigned by the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones, with the IMD as the Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre.
The Bay of Bengal experiences a much higher frequency of tropical cyclones than the Arabian Sea.
stories.mainsQuestion: Back-to-back cyclonic systems increasingly expose coastal states to repeated crop loss and slow relief. Examine how India's disaster relief financing and agrarian support mechanisms interact, and suggest reforms to make compensation for flood-linked crop damage timely and adequate.

stories.headline: NHRC notices three states over minor girls sold to middlemen
stories.summary: The National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) has issued notices to the governments of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra, along with their police chiefs, following reports that minor girls were allegedly sold to middlemen for Rs 3–5 lakh. The reports indicate the practice occurred in several districts along the states' borders. The NHRC intervention seeks accountability and action from the state authorities on the allegations. The matter raises concerns about child trafficking, weak protection mechanisms and gaps in inter-state coordination. It also highlights the NHRC's role in monitoring human rights violations and prompting state compliance.
stories.whyItMatters: Useful for GS-II social justice and GS-III internal security questions on child trafficking, NHRC's powers and state accountability. It also links human rights enforcement with federal coordination in law-and-order matters.

perspectives.take: Frames the NHRC notices as a child-rights intervention against the alleged sale of minor girls in three states, highlighting law-enforcement gaps in border districts.

articles.title: NHRC notice to 3 states, police chiefs over minor girl children being ‘sold’ to middlemen
articles.snippet: New Delhi, Nov 3 (PTI) The NHRC on Tuesday said it has issued notices to Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra governments and their police chiefs over reports that a large number of minor girl children are being allegedly sold for Rs 3-5 lakh by their parents to middlemen in several districts along the borders of…

static.topic: NHRC and Child Rights Protection
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Statutory Bodies; Social Justice — Child Rights
static.whatIsIt: The National Human Rights Commission is a statutory watchdog established under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. It can take cognizance of human rights violations, issue notices to governments and police, and recommend remedial action.
static.background: The NHRC was created in 1993 and amended in 2019. It functions as a recommendatory body, not a court, and works with State Human Rights Commissions and other agencies. Child rights are protected under constitutional provisions and special laws such as the JJ Act, 2015 and POCSO Act, 2012.
static.socioEconomic: Child trafficking is driven by poverty, gender discrimination, migration, illiteracy and weak enforcement; border districts often face gaps in inter-state coordination.
static.whyInNews: The NHRC issued notices to Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra and their police chiefs over reports of minor girls being sold to middlemen.
static.wayForward: Strengthen district child protection units, anti-trafficking units, interstate intelligence sharing, victim rehabilitation and fast-track trials; ensure timely compliance with NHRC recommendations.
prelimsPointers: NHRC is a statutory body, not a constitutional one.
It can recommend compensation, prosecution or other relief but cannot punish.
Child trafficking is prohibited under Article 23 of the Constitution.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the effectiveness of the NHRC and state machinery in preventing child trafficking and protecting vulnerable minors.

static.topic: Human Trafficking as an Internal Security Challenge
static.syllabusNode: Security — Organized Crime and Internal Security
static.whatIsIt: Human trafficking is the recruitment, transportation, harbouring or receipt of persons by force, fraud or coercion for exploitation. It is an organized crime that affects internal security, public order and human rights.
static.background: India addresses trafficking through the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act, 1956, the JJ Act, 2015, the POCSO Act, 2012 and provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour. The MHA and state police handle anti-trafficking operations.
static.geography: Border districts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra are mentioned in the reports.
static.socioEconomic: Trafficking networks exploit poverty, gender inequality, migration and weak social protection; border areas can facilitate movement and evade detection.
static.whyInNews: NHRC notices follow reports of minor girls being sold for Rs 3–5 lakh by parents to middlemen in border districts.
static.wayForward: Use a development-plus-security approach: improve education, livelihood and social security; strengthen anti-trafficking units, border policing, cyber surveillance and victim-witness protection.
prelimsPointers: Article 23 prohibits human trafficking and forced labour.
ITPA, 1956 is the primary law on immoral traffic; POCSO and JJ Act protect children.
The MHA is the nodal ministry for anti-trafficking measures.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how trafficking in persons challenges internal security and examine the adequacy of India's legal and institutional response.

prelims: NHRC issued notices to Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Maharashtra governments and their police chiefs.
Reports allege minor girls were sold to middlemen for Rs 3–5 lakh in districts along state borders.
NHRC is a statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.
Child trafficking is prohibited under Article 23 of the Constitution.
stories.mainsQuestion: Child trafficking is often described as a crime rooted in socio-economic vulnerability. In light of recent NHRC interventions, examine the effectiveness of India's legal and institutional framework in protecting minor girls from trafficking.

stories.headline: Study: Global wildlife trade involves over 107,000 species
stories.summary: A new study estimates that global wildlife trade involves more than 107,000 species of wild animals, plants and fungi, roughly twice previous estimates. It points to major monitoring gaps, especially for invertebrates and fungi, which are often overlooked in trade data. The findings raise concerns about biodiversity loss, disease transmission and invasive species spread. The study suggests current regulatory and surveillance systems may undercount the scale and diversity of species entering trade.
stories.whyItMatters: For UPSC, it links biodiversity conservation, CITES implementation, invasive species and pandemic risk to global environmental governance and India's wildlife protection regime.

perspectives.take: Frames the study as evidence of underestimated trade and weak monitoring, with emphasis on overlooked invertebrates and fungi and risks to biodiversity and health.

articles.title: Global wildlife trade involves more than 107,000 species, twice previous estimates: Study
articles.snippet: A new study reveals over 107,000 species of wild animals, plants, and fungi are traded globally, more than double previous estimates. The findings highlight significant gaps in monitoring systems, particularly for invertebrates and fungi, raising concerns about biodiversity loss, disease transmission, and invasive…

static.topic: Global wildlife trade and biodiversity conservation
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Biodiversity & Conservation
static.whatIsIt: Wildlife trade refers to the commercial exchange of wild animals, plants and fungi and their products. It is regulated internationally by CITES and domestically in India by the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972 and Biological Diversity Act 2002.
static.background: India is a megadiverse country and party to the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992) and its Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022). Domestic conservation frameworks include the Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Forest Conservation Act 1980 and Biological Diversity Act 2002. Project Tiger (1973) and Project Elephant (1992) anchor species conservation.
static.geography: Global; India is one of 17 megadiverse countries with biodiversity hotspots in the Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka and Sundaland/Nicobar.
static.socioEconomic: Wildlife trade can support livelihoods, but unregulated trade threatens ecosystems, public health and invasive species management.
static.whyInNews: A new study estimates over 107,000 species are involved in global wildlife trade, more than double previous estimates, highlighting monitoring gaps.
static.wayForward: Strengthen species-level trade monitoring, include invertebrates and fungi, improve CITES implementation and domestic enforcement, and integrate biodiversity and health risk assessments.
prelimsPointers: India's biodiversity hotspots: Himalaya, Indo-Burma, Western Ghats-Sri Lanka, Sundaland/Nicobar.
World Wetlands Day: 2 February.
CITES regulates international trade in endangered species.
static.mainsAngle: Balancing conservation with development and community rights (FRA); human-wildlife conflict management; and strengthening global governance of wildlife trade.

prelims: The study estimates global wildlife trade involves more than 107,000 species, over twice previous estimates.
Monitoring gaps are especially pronounced for invertebrates and fungi.
Concerns include biodiversity loss, disease transmission and invasive species.
stories.mainsQuestion: Discuss the implications of the underestimated scale of global wildlife trade for biodiversity conservation and international regulatory frameworks such as CITES. How can India strengthen its domestic response?

stories.headline: NPPA trims MRP of 1,085 anti-cancer drugs in revised list
stories.summary: The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has issued an updated list showing reduced maximum retail prices for 1,085 anti-cancer medicines, a revision built on price information filed by pharmaceutical companies up to 3 November. The exercise is part of the regulator's continuing effort to bring down the cost of cancer therapy by squeezing margins and aligning brand prices to ceiling levels rather than by altering the underlying molecules on the market. Because the list is periodically refreshed as companies submit fresh data, the count of affected products and their revised MRPs can change with each update. The move is expected to lower the out-of-pocket burden for patients on long-duration oncology treatment, while raising compliance and reporting obligations for manufacturers and marketers.
stories.whyItMatters: Drug price control is a standing UPSC theme linking the regulator NPPA, the DPCO 2013 framework and the health-affordability debate, especially for high-cost non-communicable disease therapies such as oncology. It allows questions on how ceiling pricing, trade margin rationalisation and the National List of Essential Medicines interact with industry viability and patient access.

perspectives.take: A business daily framing the development as a routine, data-driven regulatory update — it foregrounds that the revised list is based on company submissions up to 3 November and stresses market and compliance implications rather than patient outcomes.

articles.title: NPPA updates list of reduced MRP of 1,085 anti-cancer drugs
articles.snippet: Revised list reflects information submitted by pharmaceutical companies up to November 3

static.topic: National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) and the DPCO, 2013
static.syllabusNode: Government Policies and Interventions — Health; Statutory and Regulatory Bodies
static.whatIsIt: The NPPA is the national regulator that fixes and revises the prices of scheduled formulations and monitors the prices of all other medicines to check unreasonable profiteering. It derives its powers from the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO), 2013, which is issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
static.background: Drug price control in India dates back to the Drugs (Prices Control) Order of 1970, preceded by earlier orders from the 1960s. The Hathi Committee (1975) argued for a shift towards essential medicines and public-sector production. Successive orders — 1979, 1987, 1995 and finally DPCO 2013 — progressively moved the system from a cost-plus, cost-of-production approach towards market-based ceiling prices. The NPPA was set up in 1997 as an independent body under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, to administer the price-control regime.
static.geography: India (union-level regulation; state drug controllers assist in enforcement and compliance monitoring)
static.socioEconomic: Price control directly shapes household out-of-pocket health spending, which remains a large share of total health expenditure in India, and affects the commercial viability of manufacturers, particularly smaller formulators.
static.whyInNews: The NPPA has published an updated list showing reduced maximum retail prices for 1,085 anti-cancer drugs, based on information submitted by pharmaceutical companies up to 3 November.
static.wayForward: Periodic publication of transparent, machine-readable price lists, stronger state-level enforcement, and timely updating of the National List of Essential Medicines would improve both compliance and patient awareness of revised prices.
prelimsPointers: NPPA is an autonomous body under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, established in 1997.
DPCO 2013 is issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955; it gives NPPA powers to fix ceiling prices of scheduled formulations.
Ceiling price is computed from the average price to retailer of all brands with at least 1% market share, plus a 16% retailer margin, and is revised annually in line with WPI.
For non-scheduled formulations, manufacturers cannot increase the MRP by more than 10% in a given year.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how the ceiling-price mechanism under DPCO 2013 balances the twin objectives of affordable access and a commercially sustainable pharmaceutical industry.

static.topic: Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) in medicines
static.syllabusNode: Government Policies and Interventions — Health; Pricing and Regulation of Essential Goods
static.whatIsIt: TMR is a regulatory approach in which the government caps the margin earned across the distribution chain, calculated on the price at the first point of sale, instead of fixing a ceiling price based on cost of production. It targets the gap between the manufacturer's price and the price paid by the patient.
static.background: NPPA applied trade margin rationalisation to 42 anti-cancer non-scheduled formulations in 2019, capping the trade margin at 30% on the MRP at the first point of sale. The approach was subsequently extended to selected medical devices as well, and has been used in later exercises to bring down patient prices of high-value therapies without disturbing the underlying price-control classification of the molecules.
static.socioEconomic: TMR addresses the distribution-layer mark-up that inflates prices of non-scheduled medicines; it benefits patients but compresses margins for wholesalers, distributors and hospital pharmacies, which may affect stocking behaviour in some segments.
static.whyInNews: The reduction in MRP of 1,085 anti-cancer drugs announced by NPPA is an outcome of the margin-rationalisation approach applied to oncology medicines.
static.wayForward: Extending TMR to more high-cost therapeutic categories, coupled with monitoring of availability and stock-outs, would prevent price relief from translating into access failure.
prelimsPointers: Trade margin rationalisation caps margins on the price at the first point of sale rather than fixing a cost-based ceiling price.
NPPA's 2019 TMR order applied a 30% margin cap to 42 anti-cancer non-scheduled formulations.
TMR was later extended to selected medical devices, making it a template for high-value therapy price reduction.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether trade margin rationalisation is a more effective tool than ceiling pricing for making high-cost therapies affordable in India.

static.topic: Cancer care and medicine affordability in India
static.syllabusNode: Issues Relating to Health — Non-Communicable Diseases and Access to Medicines
static.whatIsIt: India carries a substantial share of the global cancer burden, and oncology treatment — including chemotherapy, targeted therapy and supportive care — is among the most expensive categories of medical expenditure for households.
static.background: Cancer control in India has been organised through the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Cancer, Diabetes, Cardiovascular Diseases and Stroke (NPCDCS) and, more recently, through Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, which covers cancer treatment for eligible beneficiaries. Public health spending on oncology has historically been supplemented heavily by private, out-of-pocket expenditure.
static.geography: India; the burden and treatment capacity vary widely across states, with tertiary cancer centres concentrated in metropolitan and select state capitals.
static.socioEconomic: Long-duration oncology treatment is a leading cause of catastrophic health expenditure and distress financing among Indian households; reducing drug prices is one of the few levers that lowers cost without expanding the physical care network.
static.whyInNews: The downward revision of MRPs for 1,085 anti-cancer drugs is expected to reduce the treatment cost burden for cancer patients.
static.wayForward: Complementing price regulation with wider health-insurance coverage, generic substitution, public procurement through pooled tenders and expansion of day-care chemotherapy facilities would address affordability and access together.
prelimsPointers: Non-communicable diseases, including cancer, account for the majority of deaths in India.
NPCDCS is the national programme for prevention and control of cancer and other major non-communicable diseases.
Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY provides health cover that includes cancer treatment for eligible families.
static.mainsAngle: Price regulation alone cannot solve the affordability challenge in cancer care. Critically examine this statement with reference to India's health financing and oncology infrastructure.

prelims: NPPA is an autonomous body under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, set up in 1997; it administers the DPCO, 2013, issued under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955.
Scheduled formulations (those listed in the NLEM) are subject to ceiling prices; non-scheduled formulations cannot have their MRP raised by more than 10% in a year.
Ceiling price is derived from the average price to retailer of brands with at least 1% market share, plus a 16% retailer margin, revised annually using the Wholesale Price Index.
NPPA has used trade margin rationalisation — capping margins at 30% on the price at the first point of sale — to cut prices of high-cost therapies, beginning with anti-cancer medicines in 2019.
stories.mainsQuestion: The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority has periodically revised downward the MRPs of anti-cancer medicines. Examine how far such price-control measures address the affordability of cancer treatment in India, and suggest complementary policy measures.

onThisDay.title: Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, becomes Prime Minister of Piedmont-Sardinia
onThisDay.description: Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, became the prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, a kingdom that soon expanded to become Italy. He was a key architect of Italian unification under the House of Savoy.

onThisDay.title: Soviet troops enter Hungary to crush the Hungarian Revolution
onThisDay.description: Soviet troops entered Hungary to end the Hungarian Revolution against Soviet control, which had begun on October 23. Thousands were killed, many wounded, and nearly a quarter million fled the country.
onThisDay.upscLink: Cold War; Soviet intervention in Eastern Europe.

onThisDay.title: Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin assassinated
onThisDay.description: Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated by Yigal Amir, an extremist Israeli opposed to the Oslo peace process. The killing shocked the world and complicated the Israel-Palestine peace efforts.
onThisDay.upscLink: Israel-Palestine conflict; Oslo Accords; West Asia peace process.

onThisDay.title: Jane Goodall observes chimpanzees creating tools
onThisDay.description: At the Kasakela Chimpanzee Community in Tanzania, Jane Goodall observed chimpanzees creating and using tools, the first-ever observation of tool-making in non-human animals. This discovery redefined the understanding of animal intelligence and human uniqueness.
